paragraphs.title: Summoning the Officials for the City’s Punishment

easy.q: How many men came to the Temple?

easy.explanation: Each man carried a weapon of slaughter or destruction.
easy.q: What did the men have in their hands?

easy.explanation: The man in linen had “a writer’s inkhorn by his side.”
easy.q: What did the man clothed in linen carry?

medium.explanation: They went in and stood beside the brasen altar.
medium.q: Where did the men stand after they entered?

medium.explanation: Their weapons were instruments of slaughter and judgment.
medium.q: What was the purpose of the men’s weapons?

medium.explanation: He was dressed in linen and carried a writer’s inkhorn.
medium.q: What distinguished the man clothed in linen from the other men?

answers: A formal mission of judgment had begun
The men were sent to rebuild the city
challenge.explanation: The command summons officials to carry out judgment against the city.
challenge.q: What does the command to those who had charge over the city show?

answers: To emphasize his distinct role and status
To show that he was an ordinary soldier
challenge.explanation: His linen clothing and inkhorn distinguish his special assignment.
challenge.q: Why is the man clothed in linen described separately?

answers: The command is given, the men arrive, and the linen-clad man is identified
The man marks people before anyone arrives
The city is punished before the command is given
challenge.explanation: The passage first gives the command, then describes the men arriving and the linen-clad man among them.
challenge.q: What sequence is presented in these verses?

paragraphs.title: The Departure of the Divine Glory and the Marking of the Protected

easy.explanation: The glory went up from the cherub where it had been.
easy.q: From where did the glory of the God of Israel move?

answers: To the threshold of the house
easy.explanation: It moved to the threshold of the house.
easy.q: Where did the glory move after leaving the cherub?

easy.explanation: The man was told to set a mark upon their foreheads.

medium.explanation: The command was given to the man clothed in linen.
medium.q: Who was commanded to mark the people?

answers: Those who rejoiced over the abominations
Those who sighed and cried over the abominations
medium.explanation: The mark was for those who grieved over the abominations being committed in the city.
medium.q: Which people were to receive the mark?

answers: To distinguish those to be spared
To show that they were soldiers
medium.explanation: The mark distinguished the people who were not to be struck.
medium.q: What was the purpose of the mark?

answers: The glory is moving toward leaving the Temple
The glory is moving deeper into the Temple
The glory is entering the city to bless it
challenge.explanation: The movement from the cherub to the threshold suggests departure from the sanctuary.
challenge.q: What does the movement of the glory to the threshold suggest?

answers: It identifies those who are to be struck
It identifies those who are not to be harmed
It identifies the officials carrying out judgment
challenge.explanation: The marked people are specifically protected from the slaughter.
challenge.q: How is the mark related to the judgment that follows?

answers: Their response to the city’s abominations mattered
Everyone carrying a weapon received a mark
Only city leaders received the mark
challenge.explanation: The passage distinguishes those who grieved over the abominations from those subject to judgment.
challenge.q: What can be learned from the fact that the mark was given to those who sighed and cried?

paragraphs.title: The Punishment Spreads from the Temple through the City

easy.explanation: They were commanded to go through the city and smite.
easy.q: What were the bearers of the slaughter weapons commanded to do?

answers: Anyone upon whom was the mark
easy.explanation: They were told not to come near anyone upon whom was the mark.
easy.q: Whom were they forbidden to harm?

easy.explanation: The command says, “begin at my sanctuary.”
easy.q: Where was the judgment to begin?

medium.explanation: They were told not to let their eye spare or have pity.
medium.q: What were the officials told not to do while striking?

answers: It was defiled and the courts were filled with the slain
medium.explanation: They were told to defile the house and fill the courts with the slain.
medium.q: What happened in the house after the judgment began?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to people who were killed.
medium.q: What does “the slain” mean in this passage?

answers: From the city to the sanctuary
From the sanctuary through the city
Only from the courtyard to the gate
challenge.explanation: The judgment begins at the sanctuary and then proceeds through the city.
challenge.q: What is the direction of the judgment’s spread?

answers: The weapon-bearers strike, while the marked people are spared
The weapon-bearers are protected, while the marked people are struck
Both groups receive the same treatment
challenge.explanation: The weapon-bearers carry out judgment, while those with the mark are protected.
challenge.q: What contrast exists between the weapon-bearers and the marked people?

answers: Judgment begins in the holy place itself
The sanctuary has no connection with the judgment
challenge.explanation: The command expressly says to begin at the sanctuary.
challenge.q: What does beginning at the sanctuary emphasize?

paragraphs.title: Ezekiel’s Cry and the Answer of Judgment

answers: He fell upon his face and cried
easy.explanation: Ezekiel fell upon his face and cried to the Lord.
easy.q: What did Ezekiel do when he saw the slaughter?

answers: The remnant of Israel would be destroyed
The city would be filled with joy
easy.explanation: He asked whether the Lord would destroy all the residue of Israel.
easy.q: What was Ezekiel afraid would happen?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “the land is full of blood.”
easy.q: What was the land full of?

answers: The iniquity of Israel and Judah was exceedingly great
The city was free from sin
medium.explanation: The Lord said that the iniquity of the house of Israel and Judah was exceeding great.
medium.q: What reason did the Lord give for the judgment?

answers: The land was full of blood and the city full of perverseness
The land was full of joy and the city full of peace
The land was empty and the city deserted
medium.explanation: The land was full of blood, and the city was full of perverseness.
medium.q: What two conditions are used to describe the land and city?

answers: The city is full of injustice and corruption
The city is full of houses
The city is full of water
medium.explanation: Perverseness describes the city’s corrupt and unjust condition.
medium.q: What does “the city is full of perverseness” mean in context?

answers: The land was full of blood, the city full of perverseness, and the people claimed that the Lord did not see
The people kept every commandment and were therefore punished
The city was empty of inhabitants
challenge.explanation: The Lord points to bloodshed, perverseness, and the people’s claim that He had forsaken the earth and did not see.
challenge.q: Which reason for judgment is stated explicitly?

answers: Their punishment corresponds to their deeds
They will be punished without regard to their deeds
challenge.explanation: The statement expresses judgment according to their own conduct.
challenge.q: What does “I will recompense their way upon their head” mean?

challenge.explanation: He says, “mine eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity.”
challenge.q: How does the Lord describe His attitude toward the judgment?

easy.explanation: The man clothed with linen reported the matter.

answers: He had done all that he was commanded
He had completed only part of the mission
He had not begun the mission
easy.explanation: He said, “I have done as thou hast commanded me.”
The man clothed in linen had an inkhorn by his side.

answers: He had completed the work entrusted to him
He had been commanded to strike everyone
He had been commanded to rebuild the Temple
medium.explanation: His report indicates that he carried out the assignment associated with his inkhorn and marking.
medium.q: How was the man’s report connected with his assignment?

answers: To the elders of the city
medium.explanation: He returned and reported to the one who had commanded him.
medium.q: To whom did the man report?

answers: I have carried out everything I was told to do
I did not understand the command
I did only what I wanted
medium.explanation: The man declares that he completed his commanded task.
medium.q: What does “I have done as thou hast commanded me” mean?

challenge.explanation: His words show that he had done what he was commanded.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the brief report at the end of the chapter?

answers: He is introduced with the inkhorn and ends by reporting that his mission is complete
He begins as an executioner and ends as a prophet
He begins outside the city and ends by rebuilding the Temple
challenge.explanation: His role is introduced through the inkhorn and concluded with his report of obedience.
challenge.q: How does the report complete the man’s role in the chapter?

answers: He marks those to be protected, while they carry out the punishment
He strikes the city, while they mark those to be protected
They have no difference in their assignments
challenge.explanation: The linen-clad man marks the protected people, while the others execute judgment.
challenge.q: What is the main difference between the linen-clad man and the bearers of the slaughter weapons?
